Test Name: ID957 | EU | Cart | Flagship - Native Express Payment Button + Order Summary in Cart Sticky Footer
Experiment description:
Control (current live cart): the cart footer is sticky — it stays pinned to the bottom of the screen. It shows the shipping line, the subtotal, and one "Continue to Checkout" button. No express payment options.

V1: the same sticky footer as in Control, plus a row of express payment options under "Continue to Checkout", labelled "or buy directly". Up to 3 options show, depending on the device and browser (Shop Pay, PayPal, Google Pay, Apple Pay). Nothing else on the cart changes.

V2: the same express payment row as V1, but the footer is no longer sticky. It sits at the end of the cart content, so people scroll to reach it. Because of this, the "You may also like" cross-sell block is always fully visible. In Control and V1 the sticky footer can cover part of it, depending on how many items are in the cart.
Hypothesis:
IF we add express payment options under the "Continue to Checkout" button in the cart footer ("or buy directly": Shop Pay, PayPal, Google Pay or Apple Pay, shown based on the device), and we test that footer both sticky (V1) and non-sticky (V2),

THEN purchase conversion rate will go up (H1) and average order value will stay flat or go up (H2),

BECAUSE express payment takes away the work of filling in a form at the exact moment people are most ready to buy. Decisive shoppers can skip the steps completely. Hesitant shoppers get an easier, safer-feeling way to finish: a payment sheet with Face ID, Touch ID and a saved card beats typing card details into a web form, and the wallet logos are familiar. THEN Purchase conversion rate will increase (H1) and Add to cart will hold steady (H2), even though the variant has no direct add option on this screen,

Supporting evidence
- Recognition over recall — "All Bundles" and "Build your own bundle" are both abstract; imagery and concrete descriptors ("For sleep, calm, festivals and more") give shoppers something to match against their own intent.

THEN conversion rate will remain flat while bundle entry rate and BYOB/pre-made split hold or improve,

Test Name: ID963 | EU | PLP | Flagship - PLP Entry Page — "What Brings You Here?" (Product State vs. Need State)
Experiment description:
Placement: New intermediary entry page inserted before the "All Products" PLP — shoppers land here first instead of going straight into the full product grid.
What the change will be: Control: shoppers navigating to "All Products" land directly on the current PLP grid. Variant: shoppers land on a new entry page titled "What brings you here?" with a toggle between two states — "Shop by product" (category tiles: All, Earplugs, Sleep masks, Baby earmuffs, Bundles, Accessories, Limited editions, Collaborations) and "Shop by need" (situational tiles: keep the same as HP test). Tapping any tile routes the shopper to a pre-filtered PLP matching that category or need. No changes to the PLP itself beyond the filter state on entry.
Hypothesis:
IF we insert a "What brings you here?" entry page with a Product/Need toggle before the full PLP, letting shoppers self-select a category or situational need before seeing any products,

THEN we will see an increase in PLP → PDP click-through rate and downstream Purchase conversion rate, particularly among situational, low-intent browsers,

BECAUSE pre-filtering by need reduces choice overload (Hick's Law) for the ~80% of traffic that arrives without a clear product in mind, and matching entry to why someone is shopping (rather than what they already know they want) gives Rejector-type visitors a relevant, low-effort starting point instead of an undifferentiated grid of 8+ product categories.
Additional metrics: CTR of toggle, CTR to PLP

Test Name: ID1018 | EU | Bundle PDP | Flagship - Earplug Bundle PDP redesign
Experiment description:
Control: Current Earplug bundle PDP on the legacy template — not aligned with the flagship design system

Variant: Earplug bundle PDP rebuilt on the flagship design system — the same components, hierarchy, and visual language being rolled out consistently across all flagship pages — with bundle-specific adaptations layered on top to handle multi-product presentation:
- Flagship-standard layout components (image treatment, typography, CTA style, trust signals, proof placement) — consistent with every other page in the redesign, not bespoke to this page
- Bundle-specific additions the flagship base template doesn't need to handle: per-product breakdown rows (image, name, variant/color selection per item), bundle savings framing, and a single unified add-to-bag action across multiple SKUs
Hypothesis:
IF we rebuild the Earplug bundle PDP on the flagship design system — consistent layout, hierarchy and proof placement with the rest of the site — and add the bundle-specific structure needed to present multiple products clearly (per-item breakdown, savings framing, unified CTA),
 THEN we will see an increase in Purchase CR and bundle ATC, with AOV holding or improving,
 BECAUSE two mechanisms stack here. First, consistency reduces cognitive load (BOOM Day 1, Ability) — a shopper who's already built a mental model of "how Loop PDPs work" elsewhere on the flagship site doesn't have to re-learn a different pattern on the legacy bundle template; less re-orientation effort means less drop-off before they even get to evaluating the bundle. Second, the bundle-specific structure adds Certainty (BOOM Day 4) at the exact point of hesitation unique to multi-product pages — the implicit "what exactly am I getting, and is it worth it vs. buying separately" calculation that a single-SKU-shaped page can't answer.

Archetype framing:
- Decisive buyers benefit most from the consistency piece — no friction from an unfamiliar layout breaking flow between browsing and this page.
- Maximizers benefit most from the bundle-specific piece — the per-item value breakdown gives them the buy-together-vs-separately comparison they're already trying to run mentally, so they resolve it instead of tabbing away.
- Curious shoppers benefit from both — a familiar page structure lowers the barrier to comparing this bundle against other products they've already seen on-site.

Test Name: ID1036 | USA | PDP | Flagship Yotpo follow-up
Experiment description:
Control vs V1 — what changed
Three things added at the top
- AI "Customers say" summary paragraph
- "Read summary by topics" button
- "Reviews with media" photo carousel (2 photos, swipe)
Five things moved to the bottom — from above the reviews to below the reviews and below pagination
- Search reviews box
- Rating dropdown
- With media toggle
- Popular topics pills
- Sort by
Star bars moved down
- Now sit directly above the review list — the intended fix
- Tapping a row re-renders the list right underneath it
- But the proof it worked (active filter state, "We found X matching reviews / Clear filters") now renders at the bottom, out of sight
Background: why a follow-up
ID922 / ID923 / ID924 tested a compressed Yotpo review module on mobile PDPs — padding trimmed, first-page reviews cut from 5 to 3, AI "Customers say" summary added, media gallery enabled, ear-tip-size filter added — and lost in all three markets (purchase CR −2.1% EU, −1.3% USA, −6.5% AUS). The single most consistent finding was that review-filter engagement fell 26.9% in EU, 26.5% in USA and 31.4% in AUS: same direction, same magnitude, three independent samples.

Post-test inspection of the module points at a specific cause. The star-rating distribution is itself a filter — tapping the "3 star" row filters the review list — but in that variant it sat above the AI summary and the media gallery, roughly a full mobile screen away from the reviews it controls. A shopper tapping a star row saw nothing change, because everything that changed was off-screen. An action whose consequence is invisible reads as a broken control: people try it once, conclude it does not work, and stop. That removes the self-service route to the specific reviews that resolve a specific objection — fit being the most-discussed topic in Loop reviews at 11% of all reviews, and explicitly flagged as mixed by Yotpo's own summary.

This test holds the content of the module constant and changes only the sequence: AI summary, then media gallery, then the rating distribution, then the review list. Tapping a star row now visibly re-renders the reviews directly beneath it, within the same viewport. If the hypothesis is accurate, filter interaction should recover toward or above the original module's level, and the conversion and add-to-cart losses from ID922–924 should close.

Two things to keep in mind when reading the result. Control is the original module, not the ID922 variant — so V1 differs from control on content and order. The order-only comparison is this test against ID922 / ID923. And alongside the reorder, the review search box, the filter controls and the keyword topic pills no longer sit above the review list; the AI summary and media gallery take that space instead. So the test also swaps a self-service layer for an AI-served one, and that may act on the same behaviour described above — from a different direction.
Hypothesis:
IF: we move the star-rating distribution directly above the review list on mobile PDPs, so the AI summary and media gallery sit above it rather than between it and the reviews,
THEN: rating-filter interaction will recover, and add-to-cart rate (h2) and purchase conversion rate (h1) will hold or improve,
BECAUSE: the distribution bars are filter controls, and a control whose effect renders off-screen gives no feedback that it worked — shoppers read it as broken and abandon it. Placing the result in the same viewport as the control closes the action–feedback loop, restoring the fastest route to the reviews that answer a shopper's specific doubt.
Additional metrics: Purchase CvR for segment who scrolled to the review section (trigger on customer reviews title)

Test Name: ID954 | EU | Homepage | Homepage Hero Format — Carousel vs. Stacked vs. Hybrid
Experiment description:
The current homepage hero is a single carousel slot — one campaign banner visible at a time (e.g. Halo, then Tomorrowland x Experience, then McLaren Racing), with the visitor needing to swipe or wait for auto-rotation to see the others. This test isolates hero format as the sole variable — same banners, same copy, same imagery, same order — testing two alternative structures against the current carousel:
- Control: Current live carousel — one hero visible, swipe/dot-nav to reveal others
- Variant 1 (Stacked): All hero banners rendered as separate full-width blocks, stacked vertically one after another (Halo → Tomorrorland x Experience → McLaren Racing), each fully visible without interaction, followed by bestsellers block below.
- Variant 2 (Hybrid): First/primary hero banner keeps its current prominent single-banner treatment, with the remaining hero banners presented as a carousel/slider directly below it (rather than stacked or hidden behind swipe), followed by bestsellers block below that.
Hypothesis:
IF we replace the current single-carousel hero with either a fully stacked format (V1) or a primary-hero-plus-secondary-slider hybrid (V2),

THEN we will see increased click-through to secondary campaign banners (H2) and, if that traffic is incremental rather than redistributed, a lift in purchase CVR (H1),

BECAUSE a carousel hides all but one campaign behind an interaction most visitors never make (carousel blindness) — campaigns like McLaren Racing or Tomorrowland x Experience currently get near-zero exposure unless a visitor happens to swipe. Making all campaigns visible at rest (V1) or at least reachable without a full swipe cycle (V2) removes an ability/visibility barrier, not a motivation or content barrier.

H1 (Primary): Purchase CVR

Test Name: ID955 | USA | Homepage | Homepage Hero Format — Carousel vs. Stacked vs. Hybrid
Experiment description:
The current homepage hero is a single carousel slot — one campaign banner visible at a time (e.g. Halo, then Tomorrowland x Experience, then McLaren Racing), with the visitor needing to swipe or wait for auto-rotation to see the others. This test isolates hero format as the sole variable — same banners, same copy, same imagery, same order — testing two alternative structures against the current carousel:
- Control: Current live carousel — one hero visible, swipe/dot-nav to reveal others
- Variant 1 (Stacked): All hero banners rendered as separate full-width blocks, stacked vertically one after another (Halo → Tomorrorland x Experience → McLaren Racing), each fully visible without interaction, followed by bestsellers block below.
- Variant 2 (Hybrid): First/primary hero banner keeps its current prominent single-banner treatment, with the remaining hero banners presented as a carousel/slider directly below it (rather than stacked or hidden behind swipe), followed by bestsellers block below that.
Hypothesis:
IF we replace the current single-carousel hero with either a fully stacked format (V1) or a primary-hero-plus-secondary-slider hybrid (V2),

THEN we will see increased click-through to secondary campaign banners (H2) and, if that traffic is incremental rather than redistributed, a lift in purchase CVR (H1),

BECAUSE a carousel hides all but one campaign behind an interaction most visitors never make (carousel blindness) — campaigns like McLaren Racing or Tomorrowland x Experience currently get near-zero exposure unless a visitor happens to swipe. Making all campaigns visible at rest (V1) or at least reachable without a full swipe cycle (V2) removes an ability/visibility barrier, not a motivation or content barrier.

H1 (Primary): Purchase CVR
 H2 (Confirmatory): CTR per individual hero banner (not carousel-level) — this is the number that actually tells you whether V1/V2 surfaced previously-hidden campaigns, or just reshuffled clicks that would've happened anyway
Analysis results overview:
Purchase conversion rate (H1):
 The two variants split. V2 trends positive, V1 trends negative.
- V1 (Stacked): 11.47% → 11.15%, -2.8%, 27% chance to win.
- V2 (Hybrid): 11.47% → 11.79%, +2.8%, 73% chance to win.
Hero banner CTR (H2):
 V2 lifts cards 1–2 strongly. Cards 3–4 lose clicks compared to the carousel.
- Total hero clicks per user: 5.9% control → 9.6% V2 (1.6x) → 15.7% V1 (2.6x).
- V2 per card: Paris Hilton +78%, Archive Sale +113% (both 100%). Eclipse -38% (2%). Amnesia Ibiza -64% (3%). Evergreen and Tomorrowland flat.
- V2: 83% of hero clicks land on cards 1–2.
- V1: Evergreen goes from 1.03% to 4.13% (4x).
Add to cart rate:
 Conclusive lift for V2.
- V1: +0.5%, 55% chance. ← flat
- V2: +5.8%, 93% chance.
AOV:
 Flat on both.
- V1: $69.51 vs $68.34, +1.7%, 73% chance. ← flat
- V2: $68.01 vs $68.34, -0.5%, 50% chance. ← flat
RPU:
 Positive trend for V2. Not conclusive.
- V1: $7.75 vs $7.84, -1.1%, 39% chance.
- V2: $8.02 vs $7.84, +2.3%, 71% chance.
Checkout rate:
 V2 just above the threshold.
- V1: -1.1%, 39% chance. ← flat
- V2: +3.1%, 81% chance.
PDP visit rate:
 Down for V2.
- V1: +0.3%, 57% chance. ← flat
- V2: -1.7%, 14% chance.
PLP visits per user:
 Conclusive lift on both.
- V1: +9.1%, 100% chance.
- V2: +8.5%, 100% chance.
Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendation: Iterate. Stop V1 (Stacked). Take V2 (Hybrid) into the follow-up test with shorter, more directive cards, a new card order and an auto-timer, before it goes into the Flagship homepage.
    - Neither format passes "do no harm" yet.Pooled across all three markets: V1 -1.2%, V2 -1.3% CR, about a 70% chance of being worse.
    - Pooled, each arm has more than 2,500 transactions.
    - This is not proven harm, but it is not safe enough to launch either.
    - EU blocks the launch.V2 is -3.4% in our biggest market (11% chance to win).
    - USA (+2.8%) and AUS (+3.0%) trend positive.
    - More hero clicks do not mean more orders.V2 doubles hero clicks in EU and USA.
    - Those clicks go to PLPs (+2% to +9%), not to purchases.
    - EU uses the hero least.3.3% of EU users click the hero, vs 5.9% in USA.
    - EU shoppers mostly use the menu: the nav drawer touches about 15x more sales than the hero.
    - So in EU, a taller hero mostly pushes other journeys further down ("What brings you here?", bestsellers).
    - Only about 1 in 5 visitors reach the bestseller block. The push-down is estimated from heatmap data, not measured.
    - The side-scroll row only works for the first two cards.About 80% of V2 hero clicks go to cards 1–2 in every market.
    - Cards 3–6 lose clicks compared to the auto-rotating carousel.
    - An auto-timer is needed for the later cards to be seen at all.
    - The demand for the later cards is real.When all cards were visible (V1), Evergreen got 3–7x more clicks.
    - But those clickers bought about half as often as Paris Hilton or Eclipse clickers (12% vs 20%). Order the cards by revenue per click, not by clicks.
    - Keep the second CTA on the top slide.It gets 71% of the main CTA's clicks and converts at a similar rate.
    - The follow-up test targets exactly these issues:shorter cards, so less push-down (V2);
    - product CTAs on the cards, so more directive;
    - a new card order;
    - an auto-timer, so later cards get seen.
Management summary: The hybrid hero doubled clicks but trended negative in EU, where shoppers use the hero least, so we're testing shorter, more directive cards before it goes into the Flagship homepage.
Key Results: "Run 14 experiments on flagship elements (visual, copy, interactions) across key high-traffic templates (e.g. homepage, PDP, navigation)"

Test Name: ID1035 | EU | PDP | Flagship Yotpo follow-up
Experiment description:
Control vs V1 — what changed
Three things added at the top
- AI "Customers say" summary paragraph
- "Read summary by topics" button
- "Reviews with media" photo carousel (2 photos, swipe)
Five things moved to the bottom — from above the reviews to below the reviews and below pagination
- Search reviews box
- Rating dropdown
- With media toggle
- Popular topics pills
- Sort by
Star bars moved down
- Now sit directly above the review list — the intended fix
- Tapping a row re-renders the list right underneath it
- But the proof it worked (active filter state, "We found X matching reviews / Clear filters") now renders at the bottom, out of sight
Background: why a follow-up
ID922 / ID923 / ID924 tested a compressed Yotpo review module on mobile PDPs — padding trimmed, first-page reviews cut from 5 to 3, AI "Customers say" summary added, media gallery enabled, ear-tip-size filter added — and lost in all three markets (purchase CR −2.1% EU, −1.3% USA, −6.5% AUS). The single most consistent finding was that review-filter engagement fell 26.9% in EU, 26.5% in USA and 31.4% in AUS: same direction, same magnitude, three independent samples.

Post-test inspection of the module points at a specific cause. The star-rating distribution is itself a filter — tapping the "3 star" row filters the review list — but in that variant it sat above the AI summary and the media gallery, roughly a full mobile screen away from the reviews it controls. A shopper tapping a star row saw nothing change, because everything that changed was off-screen. An action whose consequence is invisible reads as a broken control: people try it once, conclude it does not work, and stop. That removes the self-service route to the specific reviews that resolve a specific objection — fit being the most-discussed topic in Loop reviews at 11% of all reviews, and explicitly flagged as mixed by Yotpo's own summary.

This test holds the content of the module constant and changes only the sequence: AI summary, then media gallery, then the rating distribution, then the review list. Tapping a star row now visibly re-renders the reviews directly beneath it, within the same viewport. If the hypothesis is accurate, filter interaction should recover toward or above the original module's level, and the conversion and add-to-cart losses from ID922–924 should close.

Two things to keep in mind when reading the result. Control is the original module, not the ID922 variant — so V1 differs from control on content and order. The order-only comparison is this test against ID922 / ID923. And alongside the reorder, the review search box, the filter controls and the keyword topic pills no longer sit above the review list; the AI summary and media gallery take that space instead. So the test also swaps a self-service layer for an AI-served one, and that may act on the same behaviour described above — from a different direction.
Hypothesis:
IF: we move the star-rating distribution directly above the review list on mobile PDPs, so the AI summary and media gallery sit above it rather than between it and the reviews,
THEN: rating-filter interaction will recover, and add-to-cart rate (h2) and purchase conversion rate (h1) will hold or improve,
BECAUSE: the distribution bars are filter controls, and a control whose effect renders off-screen gives no feedback that it worked — shoppers read it as broken and abandon it. Placing the result in the same viewport as the control closes the action–feedback loop, restoring the fastest route to the reviews that answer a shopper's specific doubt.
Additional metrics: Purchase CvR for segment who scrolled to the review section (trigger on customer reviews title)

Test Name: ID1012 | EU | Cart | Cart New Design Cross-Sell Block
Experiment description:
Control: Small square product thumbnail on the left, with name, colour label and colour swatch stacked to its right. Price shown as an increment ("+ €34.95") and the Add button share a row at the bottom. The thumbnail is about the same size as the product already in the cart. One card fits the width, with about a fifth of the next one showing.

Variant: A single large product card. The image is centred at the top and much bigger, sitting directly on the white card with no grey container behind it. Name, colour label and swatch move below the image, full width, with a smaller swatch. Price is shown on its own ("€34.95") rather than as an increment. The Add button is unchanged. The card is wider and taller, so barely any of the next card shows and the block reads as one product at a time. It also sits higher in the cart and takes up about a quarter more space.

Isolation note: Per your scope, the block title/headline is unchanged and the underlying recommendation logic (which products are shown) is unchanged. The only variable is the visual design of the card itself — image size/prominence, layout hierarchy, and browsing mechanic (arrows + horizontal list vs. swipe + dot pagination). Any other differences visible across the two screenshots (progress bar, USP row, Apple Pay button, "Your cart" vs "Your bag" label) are outside this test.
Hypothesis:
IF we redesign the cross-sell block from a small thumbnail with dense text into a large single product card (full changes in the description above),

THEN more shoppers will add a recommended product, lifting cart AOV (H2), while purchase conversion rate holds steady (H1). Overall add-to-cart rate as guardrail.

BECAUSE the control undersells the product at the moment someone is deciding on an impulse add. A small thumbnail with several bits of information crammed into one row makes the shopper work to take it in, and the product itself barely registers. A big image does the selling for you. That matters more here than on a product page, where people already intend to buy. Showing one product at a time may also hold attention better than a row of small cards that invites scrolling straight past.

KPI note: cross-sell add-to-cart rate was the original H1, but the sample size is too small to decide on. Only ~685 cross-sell adds per arm (out of 197k users), so the metric could only have detected a change of roughly 15% or more. The observed change was -2.9%. Reassigned to a learning metric before read-out; purchase CR takes over as H1.

Visitor archetypes most affected: Satisficers moving quickly through the cart, who are more likely to be swayed by one strong product image than by scanning a row of small ones. Likely limited effect on Rejectors who don't engage with cross-sell at all.

- Metric on add to cart of the xsell items (control & variant)

In Variation 1 the block pushes a lot of extra traffic to the PLP: PLP visits rose 62% in EU, 91% in USA and 65% in AUS. Sending people straight to a single PDP removes the comparison they still need to make.

Keep the current order. Pooled over all six variant groups (104,971 users, 36,590 clicks) the usage matches the order we tested: Sleep 10.1%, Sensitivity 9.5%, Events 8.7%, Focus 4.3%, Kids 2.2%. Move Events to first for USA only, after BFCM, so we leave the homepage alone during peak.
One thing that makes the case stronger: USA already won on conversion (+8.4%, 99% chance) with the broken PLP landing in place. Whatever the fix is worth, it is worth more than what we measured.

Take this into the final homepage test with three changes:
1. Add a variant where the usecase block sits below the bestsellers block instead of above it, so we can separate the navigation gain from the AOV loss and see whether the loss is purely a position effect.
2. Clean up the PLP landing in every variant: a title that matches the usecase that was clicked, the matching filter already selected on arrival, and the partnership and Plus products added to the range so the selection is complete.
3. Keep the current usecase order. Plan the USA switch to Events-first as a separate change after BFCM.

In Variation 2 the same problem shows up in a different shape. The categories with the most click-backs are exactly the ones where the right product is least obvious — Focus (+27% to +54%) and Sensitivity (+10% to +30%) — while Sleep (+3% to +8%) and Kids (0% to +11%) barely show it, because those have one clear answer. 1. Add a variant where the usecase block sits below the bestsellers block instead of above it, so we can separate the navigation gain from the AOV loss and see whether the loss is purely a position effect.
2. Clean up the PLP landing in every variant: a title that matches the usecase that was clicked, the matching filter already selected on arrival, and the partnership and Plus products added to the range so the selection is complete.
3. Keep the current usecase order. Plan the USA switch to Events-first as a separate change after BFCM.

Analysis results overview:

Most EU metrics are genuinely neutral — transactions (+0.70%, 67%), ATC (flat), AOV (flat) all sit in true no-signal territory, which is exactly what "do no harm" is designed to wave through. Test Name: ID986 | USA | Sitewide | Mobile nav: Help me choose relocated to level 2 (contextual placement)
Experiment description:
Move the "Help me choose" entry point out of the top-level mobile nav and place it contextually at level 2 inside both Shop by product and Shop by need, providing access to the quiz, compare and read-more routes. 

Do-no-harm: primary KPI is CvR staying flat, freeing level 1 for the new flagship IA.

Changes
- Move "Help me choose" from level 1 of the mobile nav into two level 2 panels; 
    - Add the  "Help me choose" at the foot of both Shop by product and Shop by need panels
        - The link opens the same panel as in control — no change to its contents
            - Panel gives access to the Quiz, the Compare page, and to read and learn more by need

Supporting evidence
- Baymard — mobile nav guidance favours a short, scannable top level with clear category scent; secondary/utility items competing at level 1 dilute the primary paths and increase mis-taps.
- Hick's law / choice overload — fewer top-level options reduces decision time on the most-used routes; the removed item is low-traffic relative to Shop by product/need.
- Progressive disclosure — help is surfaced at the moment of need rather than pre-emptively; contextual placement raises perceived relevance of the same CTA.
- Flagship kickoff Q1/Q4 — directly serves "help visitors find their Loop" and "decisive vs curious without friction": decisive users get an unobstructed product list, curious users get help one tap deeper.
Hypothesis:
IF we relocate the "Help me choose" entry point from level 1 to the foot of both level 2 panels, 
THEN conversion rate (h1) will remain flat while level 1 becomes simpler and guided-selling usage holds, 
BECAUSE users don't recognise a need for help before they've encountered the choice set — the same panel is more relevant one tap deeper, and a shorter level 1 lowers scan cost on the primary shopping paths.

Test Name: ID951 | EU | Homepage | Flagship - Bestseller Block Format — Carousel vs. Stacked
Experiment description: The current homepage bestseller block ("Most loved earplugs") presents products as a horizontal carousel (Slide) — one card visible at a time, swipe/arrow to advance, dot pagination indicating additional cards exist off-screen. This test isolates interaction pattern as the sole variable by testing a stacked layout (Stack), where the second product card is partially visible below the first.
Hypothesis:
IF we present the Loop Essentials bestseller block as a stacked card format instead of a horizontal carousel,

THEN we will see an increase in click-through to the featured products (H2) and downstream ATC/purchase CVR (H1),

BECAUSE carousels rely on an implicit promise that users will swipe to discover more content — but this promise is frequently broken (banner blindness / carousel fatigue means most users never interact past the first slide). A stacked format makes the existence of additional products physically visible at rest (peeking edge, offset card) without requiring an interaction to reveal it, lowering the ability threshold to discover the second product.

H1 (Primary): Purchase CVR
H2 (Confirmatory): CTR on bestseller block (tracked per-card, not block-level), plus % of sessions that engage with the second/third product at all (proxy for whether stacking actually surfaces content carousels hide)
Analysis results overview:
Conversion Rate:
Variant 1 (Carousel) showed a significant uplift in conversion rate, with an increase from 9.18% in the control group to 9.74% in the variant group (+6.1% uplift, 99% Bayesian chance). Variant 2 (Stacked) rose to 9.28% (+1.1% uplift, 67% Bayesian chance), which is below our 80% threshold and therefore not conclusive.
Transactions:
Transactions increased from 2,839 in the control group to 2,963 in Variant 1, while Variant 2 landed at 2,834. Traffic was balanced across arms at 30,921, 30,413 and 30,525 users respectively.
Average Order Value:
AOV was effectively flat in both variants. It moved from €55.02 in the control group to €55.55 in Variant 1 (+1.0% uplift, 50% Bayesian chance) and €55.82 in Variant 2 (+1.5% uplift, 50% Bayesian chance). The conversion gain is therefore not coming from larger baskets.
Revenue per User:
Variant 1 achieved a significant uplift in revenue per user, rising from €5.05 in the control group to €5.41 (+7.1% uplift, 98% Bayesian chance). Variant 2 reached €5.18 (+2.6% uplift, 65% Bayesian chance), not conclusive.
Revenue:
Total revenue increased from €156,202 in the control group to €164,584 in Variant 1 and €158,190 in Variant 2.
Product Detail View Rate:
Both variants drove significantly more users onto product pages. PDV rate rose from 54.37% in the control group to 57.48% in Variant 1 (+5.7% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance) and 56.13% in Variant 2 (+3.2% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance).
PLP Visit Rate:
Category page traffic increased significantly in both variants. PLP visits per user rose 12.2% in Variant 1 and 6.1% in Variant 2, both at 100% Bayesian chance.
Checkout Rate:
Checkout rate increased significantly in both variants, from 13.76% in the control group to 14.73% in Variant 1 (+7.0% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance) and 14.52% in Variant 2 (+5.5% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance).
Add to Cart Rate:
Add to cart rate did not move meaningfully. It went from 16.75% in the control group to 16.91% in Variant 1 (+1.0% uplift, 71% Bayesian chance) and 16.70% in Variant 2 (-0.3% uplift, 45% Bayesian chance).
Bestseller Block CTR:
Click-through on the bestseller block itself dropped substantially in both variants, from 15.62% in the control group to 9.78% in Variant 1 (-37.4%) and 13.02% in Variant 2 (-16.6%). In absolute clicks that is 4,830 in control against 2,973 and 3,973. This is the expected mechanical effect of the smaller click target and is not a Bayesian-tested goal in this report.
Learnings & recommendations:
Implement Variant 1 (Carousel) in EU, USA and AUS, exactly as tested — only the product image and product name clickable, not the full tile. We keep it that way for the big test as well. Making the tile fully clickable would ship a configuration we never measured, and the evidence suggests the smaller click target is part of why this variant wins, so we are not taking that risk now. We retest fully clickable after BFCM as its own experiment.
Learnings:
Both new formats beat the current block, so this was not a choice between a winner and a loser. Pooled across the three markets the carousel delivered +4.2% purchase CR at 98.5% Bayesian chance; the stacked format reached +1.5% at 78% and sits below our threshold. EU is a standalone winner (+6.1%, 99%), while USA and AUS lacked traffic rather than lacked the effect — every regional interval contains the pooled result. Build the business case on roughly +4%, not the +6.1% EU headline.
The clearest finding is behavioural. Both formats cut clicks into the bestseller block by 17% to 40%, yet increased product detail views by around 3 percentage points and PLP visits per user by 6% to 15%, at 100% Bayesian chance in five of six cells. The block became a worse click magnet and a better navigation entry point. USA is the internal control on that reading: the stacked variant there is the only cell where block CTR held flat, and also the only cell where PDV and PLP visits did not rise.

Test Name: ID931 | EU | BYOB | Flagship BYOB - Add Use-case filters (Noise sensitivity / Sleep / Music & events etc)
Experiment description:
Build Your Bundle (BYOB) is Loop's largest bundle route by volume, but it presents the whole catalogue as one long scrollable list with no way to narrow by need. 
Customers shop by use case, not product — so to build a use-case-relevant bundle they have to scroll the full range and already know which product solves which need. That's friction on our highest-volume bundle path. 
This test adds use-case filters to BYOB so users can view products by need, mirroring the site-wide "Shop by need" taxonomy.

- Control: BYOB shows the discount slider + full product list. No way to filter by use case.
- Variant 1 (V1): 
    - Adds a row of use-case filter chips between the discount slider and the product list. 
    - Selecting a use case (e.g. Sleep) filters the control list to relevant products. 
    - Filters and products shown: 
        - (Note, some products aren't available on BYOB control or V1 e.g. Eclipse or the Pleasing colab)
        - Noise Sensitivity: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships), Loop Link (all 3 versions)
        - Sleep: Dream, Quiet
        - Music & Events: Experience, Experience Plus, Switch (incl. Experience & Switch partnerships), Loop Link (all 3 versions)
        - Focus: Quiet, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships), Loop Link (all 3 versions)
        - Social Gatherings: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships), Loop Link (all 3 versions)
        - Parenting: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships), Loop Link (all 3 versions)
        - Travel: Quiet, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships), Loop Link (all 3 versions)
        - Playtime & Schooltime: Loop Engage Kids, Loop Link (all 3 versions)
        - Motorcycle: Experience, Experience Plus, Switch (incl. Experience & Switch partnerships), Loop Link (all 3 versions)

Build notes:
- For simplicity
    - let's allow only 1 filter at a time
    - so it can behave similar to the PLP /All filter. 
    - But note, we have an updated color styling for the filter chips when not selected, css:
        - background-color: #ffffff;
        - border: .0625rem1px solid #252427;
- Same test runs in EU & USA (not in Aus due to low traffic)

 Data & rationale
- BYOB is the single largest bundle route by volume (23,392 units in the EU Shopify pull — well ahead of any named bundle), so gains here have the most leverage.
- Most BYOB bundles are small — 2-item is the biggest segment (31%), then 6+ (19%) and 3-item (17%) — so helping users quickly find the right 2nd/3rd item for a need is where the volume sits.
- Customers shop by use case: Sleep, Noise Sensitivity and Music & Live Events are 68.5% of menu clicks; the Shop by need menu already won its test (ID827) and the PLP carries use-case filters — BYOB is the remaining gap.
- Customers combine needs — ~52% of filter behaviour is multi-use-case — so a multi-select filter fits how people build.
- The catalogue is getting large, so an unfiltered list is high cognitive load on mobile.
- Prior learning (PLP filter test ID565): forcing filters and removing shortcuts didn't lift macro KPIs and usage was ~1% — but the takeaways were don't force it, keep it additive and use-case/problem-based navigation works. BYOB differs: users here are already in active build/compare mode with high intent, and this filter is additive (nothing removed) — so it applies that learning rather than repeating it.

If If we add a use-case filter to BYOB,
then potentially more users will add their first product to the bundle (h1) and convert (h2). This is a Do No Harm test: we want h1 or h2 >20% chance to win
because use-case filters will improve control and confidence - and accelerate time to find the correct product.

This is an MVP simple solution, the final solution that's launched could include mroe complex UX (selecting multiple use-cases at once)

Experiment description:

Both variants converge on the same sticky top mechanic once the visitor scrolls deep enough; they differ in how present/persistent the ATC feels in the first viewport.

The flagship PDP redesign removes this block for a cleaner, more premium layout. Since it is a live cross-sell and value-framing mechanism, removing it blind risks suppressing bundle attach rate and AOV. This test isolates the removal on the current PDP — ahead of the full flagship migration — so its impact on AOV and sales reads cleanly, separate from every other flagship change. Bundle-PDP entries dropping is expected and is not itself the finding; the question is what happens to revenue per visitor.

Test Name: ID970 | USA | PDP | Remove Bundle & Save block
Experiment description:
The current PDP template includes a "Bundle & save" carousel surfacing curated bundles (Good Night, Daily Calm, Deluxe, Full Coverage) with anchored discount pricing directly on the single-product page. This block is not individually tracked, so its contribution to AOV and sales is inferred rather than measured. As a proxy, we measured how many PDP visitors navigate onward to a specific bundle PDP:

- Dream: 9.2% PDP visitors visit a bundle PDP
- Switch: 10,6
- Experience: 10.7
- Quiet: 10,8
- Engage: 13,5
- All average: 10.6
(see attachment image)

On average 10.6% of PDP visitors move onward to a bundle PDP, with earplug-bundle the dominant destination (54% of all click-throughs, 5.7% of all PDP traffic). This click-through path is not the block's total value — it excludes bundles bought without a bundle-PDP visit and includes visitors who would have found bundles anyway — but it establishes the block sits on a non-trivial share of the journey. The flagship PDP redesign removes this block for a cleaner, more premium layout. Since it is a live cross-sell and value-framing mechanism, removing it blind risks suppressing bundle attach rate and AOV. This test isolates the removal on the current PDP — ahead of the full flagship migration — so its impact on AOV and sales reads cleanly, separate from every other flagship change. Bundle-PDP entries dropping is expected and is not itself the finding; the question is what happens to revenue per visitor.
Hypothesis: If we remove the Bundle & save block from the PDP, then AOV (h2) and will drop while single-product CVR (h1) holds steady, because the block is currently the main way shoppers discover bundles and see their discounted value at the moment they're ready to buy.

Test Name: ID945 | EU | PDP | Flagship - Content - Full Content vs. No Content vs. Progressive Reveal
Experiment description: Testing whether removing or shortening the product description block changes purchase behaviour across all earplug PDPs (Dream, Quiet 2, Experience 2 + Plus, Engage 2 + Plus/Kids, Switch 2, McLaren Switch). Control shows the current full expandable content (benefit checklist + "show more"). Var 1 simply hides the content block — nothing else on the page changes or gets replaced; the page is shorter, everything below the block moves up. Var 2 shows only the first paragraph of the existing content, no expand/collapse, with a scroll-triggered discovery animation where text opacity shifts grey→black as the user reads down it. No other elements are added in either variant. This isolates content volume/presentation as the sole variable, holding layout, ATC placement, and Compare link position constant everywhere else on the page.
Hypothesis:
IF we hide the product description content entirely (Var 1) or shorten it to a single animated paragraph (Var 2),

THEN purchase CVR (H1) & Add to cart (H2) will hold flat or improve in Var 2 but decline in Var 1, consistently across product lines,

BECAUSE the content block currently carries reassurance signals (comfort claims, ear-tip specifics, fit guidance) that reduce pre-purchase uncertainty — a real barrier here given fit is the top negative-review driver for Dream (46%) and ANC-expectation gap is a known issue for Quiet 2 (138 reviews). Removing it outright (Var 1) strips that reassurance with nothing replacing it, which should increase hesitation or perceived risk at the point of decision (BOOM: Certainty friction). Var 2 keeps enough content to preserve the reassurance signal while reducing the reading/scanning effort (Ability friction) needed to get there; the grey-to-black animation is a light engagement mechanic that should pull more users through the shortened paragraph than they'd read of the full expandable block, without adding any new page elements.

Test Name: ID940 | USA | PDP | Flagship - Compare module design Dream vs Quiet
Experiment description:
Both control and variant show the same comparison — Dream vs. Quiet 2 — already established as the most-compared pairing. The only thing that changes is how it's presented:
- Control: the current full compare module — two dropdown selectors (pre-set to Dream / Quiet 2), star ratings, review counts, full pricing, colorway swatches, and a "Perfect For" section per product. Visitor-facing, but dense — it reads as a research tool.
- Variant: a stripped-down "Our Most-Asked Question" card — just the two products, one line of positioning each ("Perfect for all-night sleep" vs. "Perfect for napping"), and a single "Compare them" CTA. It reads as an answer, not a task.
Because the pairing is identical, this isolates format and framing as the variable: does presenting the comparison as a lightweight, pre-answered "most-asked question" reduce the effort/weight of engaging with it, versus a full comparison table that visitors have to actively read and cross-reference?

Mechanism: the control's density is useful for Maximizers who want the full data before committing, but it's a lot of visual and cognitive load to process on a PDP — reviews, colors, pricing across two products at once. That weight can suppress engagement for visitors who'd otherwise click through, especially Satisficers who just want the doubt resolved fast. The variant compresses the same information into a low-effort teaser, using the "most-asked question" framing as social proof (other buyers had this doubt) rather than presenting it as a research task.
Hypothesis:
IF: we replace the full dual-product comparison table on the PDP with a lightweight, single-CTA "Our Most-Asked Question" card — same Dream vs. Quiet 2 pairing, different format,
THEN: click-through into the comparison (H1) and downstream purchase conversion (H2) will increase,
BECAUSE: reducing the visual and cognitive weight of the module lowers the barrier to engaging with it, so more visitors act on their curiosity/doubt instead of skimming past a dense table that reads as effort rather than resolution.

Test Name: ID934 | USA | PLP | Flagship - GST - Sticky help me choose button
Experiment description: Loop's own post-purchase (KNO) survey data shows the Help Me Choose Quiz is already a meaningful part of how customers navigate the range pre-purchase, but on the Shop All / PLP grid today it's buried — there's a static "Help me choose" card mixed in among product tiles, competing for attention with 8+ products, colour swatches, ratings, and "Tap to try" prompts. This is a classic choice-overload environment: with Dream, Quiet 2, Experience 2 (Plus), Engage 2 (Plus/Kids), and Switch 2 all visible at once, undecided visitors face a wide, low-guidance choice set with no differentiation cue beyond "Primary benefit" placeholder copy. Behavioural research on choice overload (Iyengar & Lepper) shows that as the size of a choice set grows without added guidance, decision paralysis and drop-off increase — shoppers disengage rather than choose. Persisting a "Help me choose" CTA as a sticky, always-visible element (rather than one card among many) gives undecided visitors a constant low-effort escape hatch out of the comparison grid and into a guided decision path, at the exact moment choice overload would otherwise cause them to bounce.
Hypothesis:
IF: we add a sticky, persistent "Help me choose" button/pill that stays visible on screen while scrolling the Shop All PLP grid (in addition to or replacing the static in-grid card),
THEN: click-through to the Help Me Choose Quiz (H2) and downstream purchase conversion rate (H1) will increase,
BECAUSE: undecided visitors facing a wide, low-differentiation choice set experience choice overload and disengage rather than commit to a product; a persistent, always-accessible guidance CTA lowers the effort cost of resolving that uncertainty at the moment it occurs, rather than requiring them to scroll back up or hunt for it among competing product tiles.

Here's the learnings and management summary for the sticky help-me-choose test, all three markets. Third-person, prose without numbers in the learnings, one sentence for the summary.
💡 Learnings & Recommendations
What was tested: a sticky, persistent "Help me choose" button that stays visible while scrolling the PLP grid, appearing after the first product row. Today the same guidance lives as a static card buried among the product tiles; this test pulls it out into an always-available CTA. Two variants tested the destination — one leading to the Help Me Choose quiz, the other to a product-compare view — against a control with only the buried in-grid card.
Recommendation: Implement the sticky button in EU and US, where both variants delivered a strong, significant lift in purchase, order value, and revenue per visitor. Hold AUS: its negative read is most likely a small-sample, high-baseline artifact rather than evidence that guidance hurts Australian shoppers. The choice between quiz and compare can be made on maintenance cost, since the two performed near-identically everywhere.
The headline learning overturns a working assumption. Earlier in the flagship programme, guidance mechanisms looked like low-value clutter — the use-case toggle was activated by almost no one and abandoned by half of those who tried it, which suggested shoppers simply do not want navigation aids. This test shows that conclusion was too broad: it was the toggle that failed, not guidance itself. The difference is what the mechanism asks of the shopper. The toggle demanded that people re-navigate the entire page into a different mode; the sticky button offers a low-effort escape from a crowded, hard-to-differentiate grid at the precise moment hesitation sets in, without disturbing the browsing default. Test Name: ID919 | EU | PDP | Flagship - CTA anchoring Price & Text
Experiment description:
The current 'Add to cart' button on the Dream PDP doesn't include the price. Screen readers announce the button as "Add to cart", giving users no price information at the moment of commitment. We're asking them to either remember the price if they've already tabbed through it, or to tab back to find it before they commit. Adding more complexity, time and cognitive load to their journey before they've committed.

We're testing three approaches against the control:
- Variant 1: "Add to cart for £45.95" – price embedded in a single continuous phrase, reads as a complete sentence. Will be announced in full by assistive technology. centered to the right. 
- Variant 2: "£45.95 · Add to cart" – 2 distinct copy elements to tab through, not one: price first, action follows. This matches the reading direction and positions price as the first thing to confirm before committing. price left, add to cart right. 
- Variant 3: add to cart left and price right. 

Control keeps the current "Add to cart" with price displayed separately near the colour selector.

Goal: ship the accessible version that performs at or above control, and understand which price placement model works best on this surface
Hypothesis: If we add the price to the CTA button's for accessibility and pair it with a layout that ties price to the CTA (B, C, or D), then conversion for sighted users will stay at or above control, because putting the price right next to the action makes the decision easier, while leading with the price (D) puts cost front-of-mind at the exact moment someone's about to commit, which can make them hesitate.

Test Name: ID772 | EU | PLP | Flagship Use case toggle + Filter combo – regular PLP
Experiment description:
Previous PLP experiments revealed two important behavioural patterns.

First, users consistently responded to use-case and problem-based framing — Sleep, Focus, Noise. Across multiple markets, use-case categorisation influenced product selection and confirmed that meaningful need-based shopping intent already exists on the PLP. However, replacing product-based browsing entirely with use-case categorisation reduced product exploration and, in some markets, resulted in a downlift in add-to-cart rate.

Second, filter experiments showed that users actively try to refine products when given structured filters, especially with problem-based language ("Noise" outperformed "Hearing"). At the same time, forcing users into a filter-heavy journey introduced friction, fragmented navigation behaviour, and failed to improve macro conversion metrics.

Together, these experiments suggest that users want guidance and think in use cases and problems, but still want the freedom to browse and compare products directly.
This experiment introduces a hybrid PLP discovery experience that builds on both learnings:
- Product-first browsing remains the default experience
- An optional "Use cases" toggle offers a secondary navigation route for intent-driven shoppers
- A cleaner, more structured filter system is integrated into the browsing experience

The updated filter hierarchy follows a clearer decision structure: (1) Product Type, (2) Use Case, (3) Sensory refinement, (4) Color.
Critically, use case filters now surface a curated, intentional product set rather than the full catalogue. This addresses a known friction point: selecting "Noise Sensitivity" — one of our most-used filters — currently returns too many products, overwhelming users rather than guiding them. 

The curated sets are:
- Noise Sensitivity: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Sleep: Eclipse, Dream
- Music & Events: Experience, Experience Plus, Switch (incl. Experience & Switch partnerships)
- Focus: Quiet, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Social Gatherings: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Parenting: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Travel: Quiet, Eclipse, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Playtime & Schooltime: Loop Engage Kids
- Motorcycle: Experience, Experience Plus, Switch (incl. Experience & Switch partnerships)

Note: Conversation has been removed as a standalone filter given product overlap with existing use cases.

Unlike previous experiments, users are not forced into a use-case journey or a filter-first journey. They can freely browse products directly, switch into use-case navigation, or refine through filters depending on their shopping intent.
Hypothesis:
IF we introduce an optional use-case navigation layer together with a cleaner, structured filter system on the PLP — where use-case filters surface a curated, intentional product set rather than the full catalogue — while keeping product-based browsing as the default experience,
THEN Purchase Conversion Rate (H1) and Add to Cart rate (H2) will increase or remain stable, while use-case filter engagement improves,
BECAUSE users can self-select into a need-based discovery journey when relevant, while maintaining the freedom to browse and compare directly. Reducing the number of products shown after a use-case filter is selected lowers cognitive overload and eliminates the paradox of choice effect that the current experience triggers — especially for high-traffic filters like Noise Sensitivity. Users who arrive with clear intent get a shortlist; users who are still exploring retain full access to the range. This serves both shopping modes without forcing either.

The use-case toggle specifically should be treated as unproven at best and probably dead weight — worth keeping only if it costs nothing to maintain, and a candidate for removal rather than further investment. The primary KPI sits below the significance threshold, so the case for shipping rests on the guardrail pass and the revenue-per-visitor lean, not on a proven conversion win.
Management summary: The hybrid PLP held conversion flat across a full runtime — clearing the do-no-harm bar — while the use-case toggle was barely used and heavily reverted and filters drew twice the engagement, with half of filter-users stacking multiple filters, confirming for the third time that filters, not a toggle, are the container for use-case intent.

Experiment description:
Previous PLP experiments revealed two important behavioural patterns.

First, users consistently responded to use-case and problem-based framing — Sleep, Focus, Noise. Across multiple markets, use-case categorisation influenced product selection and confirmed that meaningful need-based shopping intent already exists on the PLP. However, replacing product-based browsing entirely with use-case categorisation reduced product exploration and, in some markets, resulted in a downlift in add-to-cart rate.

Second, filter experiments showed that users actively try to refine products when given structured filters, especially with problem-based language ("Noise" outperformed "Hearing"). At the same time, forcing users into a filter-heavy journey introduced friction, fragmented navigation behaviour, and failed to improve macro conversion metrics.

Together, these experiments suggest that users want guidance and think in use cases and problems, but still want the freedom to browse and compare products directly.
This experiment introduces a hybrid PLP discovery experience that builds on both learnings:
- Product-first browsing remains the default experience
- An optional "Use cases" toggle offers a secondary navigation route for intent-driven shoppers
- A cleaner, more structured filter system is integrated into the browsing experience

The updated filter hierarchy follows a clearer decision structure: (1) Product Type, (2) Use Case, (3) Sensory refinement, (4) Color.
Critically, use case filters now surface a curated, intentional product set rather than the full catalogue. This addresses a known friction point: selecting "Noise Sensitivity" — one of our most-used filters — currently returns too many products, overwhelming users rather than guiding them.

- Noise Sensitivity: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Sleep: Eclipse, Dream
- Music & Events: Experience, Experience Plus, Switch (incl. Experience & Switch partnerships)
- Focus: Quiet, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Social Gatherings: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Parenting: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Travel: Quiet, Eclipse, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)

Test Name: ID927 | AUS | PLP | Flagship - Needed review info
Experiment description:
Minimalism finetune of the star-rating display on the PLP , following the ID193/212/213 finding that star ratings are the safest CVR format. 

The current PLP shows stars + review count on each product card. This test removes the count to see whether the stars alone carry the trust signal on a listing page, where people scan fast and clutter has a cost.

Control — stars + review count (8095 Reviews); 
V1 —just  stars

Just like the PDP experiment -> goal: identify the minimum rating treatment that holds conversion, and isolate whether the review count's social-proof volume drives behaviour independently of the numeric score.
Hypothesis: If we remove the review count from the PLP cards and show only stars, then click-through to PDP and purchase will hold at or near control, because on a listing page people scan quickly and spend little time on each card. Stars work as a fast visual trust cue that earns the click at a glance, while the review count adds extra clutter that competes for attention without adding much trust at this stage — where the only decision is whether to look closer, not whether to buy.

📊 Analysis Results Overview
Purchase (order confirmation): The one significant result — and it's negative.
- Control: 6.81%

Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendation: Keep the review count on PLP cards. There is no market where removing it helped, and the click-through data shows it costs nothing to leave in place.
The hypothesis was that on a fast-scanned listing page the review count is clutter — stars earn the click at a glance, and the count competes for attention without adding trust, since the only decision there is whether to look closer. The click-through metric tests that directly, and it comes back flat in all three markets: removing the count changed how many people clicked into product pages by a fraction of a percent, nowhere near significant, even in Australia. So the "clutter that suppresses clicks" theory is not supported — the count neither helps nor hurts the click decision on the listing page. On its stated terms, the hypothesis is not confirmed.
The two high-traffic markets close the case cleanly: EU and US show no movement on click-through, add-to-cart, or purchase. Removing the count is invisible there. On that evidence alone the count looks inert on the PLP — safe to keep, pointless to remove.
Australia is the complication, but the new click-through data reframes it rather than reinforcing it. Australia lost purchase and add-to-cart significantly — yet its click-through to product pages was flat, exactly like the other two markets. If the missing count had genuinely weakened trust on the listing page, fewer people would have clicked through; instead the same share clicked through and then fewer converted further down. That decouples the conversion loss from the listing-page change itself: the drop appears after the click, on surfaces this test did not alter. Combined with Australia being the smallest and most volatile market, the most probable reading is a confound — traffic composition, an overlapping downstream test, or sampling — rather than proof that the review count drives Australian purchases from the PLP.
Taken together the decision is low-regret and clear. Keeping the count carries no measured cost on any metric in any market; removing it delivers no measured benefit anywhere and is entangled with an unexplained, probably-confounded loss in one thin market. The count stays. If it is ever revisited, it should be a properly-powered single-market retest with clean downstream attribution — not a rollout justified by two nulls and one anomaly.
Management summary: Removing the review count from PLP cards left click-through to product pages unchanged in every market — so the "count is clutter" idea doesn't hold; it did nothing in EU and US and the Australian conversion drop happened after the click, not on the listing page, so it's most likely a confound. The count stays on the cards.

Test Name: ID805 | EU | PDP | Colour swatches
Experiment description:
This experiment focuses on improving guided decision-making on the mobile PDP by restructuring how colour options are presented to users.
Across qualitative research, behavioral analysis, and experimentation learnings, three recurring themes emerged:
1. Users think in situations, not products.
2. Users validate decisions visually rather than through detailed reading.
3. Users want help choosing — not more options to browse.
The current colour selection experience places all swatches in a relatively flat hierarchy, requiring users to manually interpret which colours belong to core collections versus limited editions. This creates unnecessary cognitive effort during a high-intent decision-making moment.
The variant introduces a more guided and structured selection experience by:
- Separating core colours from limited-edition collections.
- Surfacing the active selection directly within its contextual group.
- Increasing visual hierarchy and scanability.
- Making premium and limited variants easier to recognize and validate visually.
This shifts the PDP experience from a browsing interface toward a decision-support interface.
Rather than asking users to process and compare all available options equally, the variant helps users understand:
- what category they are selecting from,
- which option is currently active,
- and which colours carry limited-edition value.
The experiment aims to reduce decision friction, improve purchase confidence, and increase add-to-cart behavior by making colour selection feel more intuitive and guided.

Strategic Research Connection
Theme 1 — From product-first to situation-first
Users are not evaluating colour variants analytically; they are trying to quickly recognize which option feels right for them. Structured grouping helps users map products to intent faster.
Theme 2 — From explanation to visual validation
Users do not read to understand — they scan to validate. The redesigned hierarchy improves visual comprehension and reduces reliance on explanatory text.
Theme 3 — From browsing to guided decision-making
The variant introduces lightweight decision guidance by organizing options into clearer mental models instead of presenting all choices equally.
Hypothesis:
If we restructure the colour selection experience by separating core colours from limited-edition collections and creating clearer visual hierarchy around the active selection,
then purchase rate (h1) and add-to-cart rate (h2) will increase,
because users currently need to browse and interpret the swatch section themselves, while research shows they instead want quick visual validation, clearer relevance cues, and more guided decision-making during product selection.

Test Name: ID883 | EU | PDP | Delete 640K legacy
Experiment description:
The current PDP contains a legacy section called “Join over 640K Loop fans” positioned above the comparison module. While the block was originally intended to provide social proof, recent 6V research indicates that it currently adds limited decision-making value for users. The section is not directly connected to product-specific use cases, does not help users better understand which product fits their needs, and does not function as a meaningful gateway to user-generated content or community engagement.

Additionally, the block interrupts the flow toward more conversion-oriented content such as product comparisons, specifications, and purchase-focused modules. On mobile especially, the section occupies a significant amount of vertical space, potentially pushing more relevant content further down the page and increasing unnecessary scrolling friction.

This experiment aims to validate whether removing the “Join over 640K Loop fans” block creates a cleaner and more focused PDP experience. By reducing non-essential content and keeping users concentrated on product-related information, we expect users to navigate more efficiently through the PDP and maintain stronger purchase intent throughout their journey. The test will help determine whether this legacy section still contributes value or whether it can safely be removed from the PDP template without negatively impacting engagement or conversion metrics.
Hypothesis: If we remove the “Join over 640K Loop fans” section from the PDP, then ATC (h2) and purchase (h1) will remain stable or improve, because users will experience a cleaner and more focused product page with less distraction from non-product-specific content that does not actively support purchase decision-making.
Dev briefing: Delete the 640K loopers block on all PDP's
Analysis results overview:
Purchase CVR (H1): Borderline significant uplift, 2.65% → 2.67% (+0.58%, 81% chance).
ATC rate (H2): No significant change, 5.78% → 5.80% (+0.2%, 71% chance).
AOV: No change, €57.22 → €57.55 (+0.6%, 50% chance).
RPU (per session): Moderate uplift, €1.52 → €1.54 (+1.1%, 76% chance). Inconclusive.
Checkout rate: No change, 4.16% → 4.16% (51% chance).
PLP visits: Significant uplift, 208,801 → 211,779 (+1.6% per session, 100% chance).
Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendation: Implement. Remove the "Join over 640K Loop fans" block in the Flagship PDP tests (mobile). In USA, don't leave the gap empty: keep product-specific social proof near the comparison module (star rating, review count, UGC per product). Watch US ATC closely in the Flagship PDP test.
- No harm to conversion in any region. EU and AU are borderline positive (81%). USA is flat. The block can go.
- In EU and AU, people moved on to products faster. PLP visits rose +1.6% (EU) and +1.7% (AU), both at 100% chance. The block took screen space and attention but did not help people choose. Less content before the decision means less scrolling.
- USA is the exception. ATC fell −1.5% (0% chance) and RPU fell −1.0% (4% chance). This only partly showed up in CVR. A likely reason: US shoppers rely more on "lots of people use this" as a trust signal, so the big number did work there. We have not proven this.
- AU earned more per user. RPU rose +2.3% (95%) and AOV +1.2%. A cleaner page did not push people to cheaper products.
- General brand proof ("640K fans") doesn't help people choose. Product-specific proof is the more likely job to keep, especially for USA.
Management summary: Removing the 640K fans block does no harm to conversion and helps EU and AU, but US shoppers add to cart less without it: remove it in the Flagship PDP and keep product-specific social proof for USA.
Key Results: "Run 14 experiments on flagship elements (visual, copy, interactions) across key high-traffic templates (e.g. homepage, PDP, navigation)"

Test Name: ID981 | EU | Quiz | Multi-Select Use Case Question on Quiz Q1
Experiment description:
Control: current live quiz Q1 allows selecting only one use case tile (Noise sensitivity, Music & events, Better sleep, Conversations & social gatherings, Focus & travel, All day noise control, Parenting, Other) before advancing. 

Variant: same question and same tiles, but shoppers can select multiple use cases before proceeding — e.g. someone can pick both "Better sleep" and "Parenting" if both apply. No changes to tile content, imagery, or order; only the selection behavior (single vs. multi) and the underlying recommendation logic needed to weight multiple inputs.
Hypothesis:
IF we allow shoppers to select multiple use cases on Quiz Q1 instead of forcing a single choice,

THEN we will see an increase in quiz completion rate and Results page → Purchase conversion rate,

BECAUSE most real buying situations aren't single-purpose (someone buying for both sleep and parenting, or noise sensitivity and travel, is common) and forcing a single pick creates artificial friction — either shoppers hesitate/abandon because no single tile feels fully accurate (choice-fit anxiety), or they pick one arbitrarily, which degrades match quality and lowers confidence in the final recommendation. Letting them select everything that's true removes that forced trade-off and should produce a more personally relevant — and more trusted — result.

Test Name: ID1002 | EU | Sitewide | Flagship Mobile Nav 2026
Experiment description:
Replace the entire mobile navigation with the 2026 flagship design: dark-themed, tabbed, with two parallel level-1 shopping routes (product-type and situation), a five-situation taxonomy, visual product cards, a sub-panel for products with a Plus version, and per-situation editorial guides.

Do-no-harm: primary KPI is CvR staying flat.

The real deliverable is an elevated nav with a full picture of nav usage in both control and v1 - every link (to a page) is ideally tracked with a query code - so the flagship IA can be validated before it becomes the redesign baseline.

Changes from Control
1. Level 1 restructured from a shop and help (guided selling) mix into two routes plus utility: Shop by product, Shop by situation, Accessories, Bundles (Save up to 20%), Shop all, and Returns & cancellations below a divider.
2. Shop by product opens an intermediate "By products" panel — Earplugs, Sleep masks, Baby earmuffs, each with thumbnail — plus Compare, Shop all and Help me choose.
    a. This is a risk, as user-journey lengthens vs Control - BUT it supports future brand growth
3. Plus becomes a variant panel, not a separate SKU row. Loop Engage and Loop Experience open their own panel with the base product and the Plus version, labelled "Includes Loop Mute", plus Shop all and Help me choose. Dream, Switch, Quiet and Engage Kids link straight to their product page.
4. Tabs added at the top of the drawer: Shop / What's new / About us (control has no tab layer). What's new carries three editorial cards — Paris Hilton x Loop Engage, Loop Eclipse, Amnesia Ibiza x Loop — ordered to match the homepage hero carousel, plus Collaborations, Limited editions, Shop all and a Partnerships section.
5. Dark theme replaces white.
6. "Shop by need" → "Shop by situation"  and the taxonomy collapses from nine to five: Sleep, Focus, Noise sensitivity, Events & music, Kids.
7. Situation panels become visual: product cards with imagery and one-line descriptors, plus Compare and Shop all. Situation panels link to base products only — no variant drill-down.
8. Editorial guides added at the foot of situation panels: Sleep guide + White noise generator (Sleep), Work & study guide (Focus), Parenting guide + Noise sensitivity guide (Noise sensitivity), Concert guide + Festival guide (Events & music), Kids' hearing guide (Kids). No read-time labels.     
9. "Help me choose" is a persistent CTA button at the fo        ot of the By products, Earplugs, Loop Engage, Loop Experience and By situation panels — five placements. Not on level-3 situation panels.
10. Products labelled by benefit in the Earplugs panel: Dream–Restful sleep, Engage–Easier conversations, Experience–Clearer live music, Switch–Adjustable control, Quiet–Deep noise reduction, Engage Kids–Ages 6–12.
11. Product naming: 
    a. full "Loop [Name]™" format,
    b. The "2" number in the names are dropped - we no longer need the generation suffixes 
12. Bundles opens a panel with two NON visual items - using the same copy as Control:
    a. Build your own bundle
        i. Mix and match to save
        ii. Points to /products/build-your-bundle
    b. All Bundles
        i. Our most-loved bundles
        ii. Points to /collections/bundles

    a. Stores, 
    b. locale switcher, currency switcher
        i. clicking any of the 3 local items will open the same modal that opens from the header Flag on control

Data - Supporting evidence
- Recognition over recall — product imagery in nav panels lets shoppers identify by appearance rather than decoding names; strongest where SKU names are non-descriptive (Quiet, Switch, Engage all read as abstract).
- Hick's law / category-logic consistency (Baymard) — nine mixed entries (need + context + attribute) → six single-logic entries reduces scan and disambiguation cost.
- Dual-path IA (Flagship kickoff Q4, decisive vs. curious) — product-type at level 1 serves the decisive shopper; Shop by situation and the Help me choose CTA serve the curious without diverting the primary path.
- Scalable architecture (Q6) — Earplugs / Sleep masks / Baby earmuffs as top-level categories is the structure that absorbs new lines without another IA rebuild. Eclipse and Halo currently sit awkwardly inside an earplug-shaped nav.
- Editorial in nav is a known risk — content links inside a shopping drawer are a documented diversion vector. These need their own guardrail, not just a CvR floor.
Hypothesis:
IF we replace the current mobile nav with the flagship 2026 design, 

THEN conversion rate will remain flat - validating the new Flagship nav design

BECAUSE the IA gives decisive shoppers a product route and undecided shoppers a situation route and Help me choose at relevant placements, instead of one mixed list; visual cards let people recognise products rather than decode names; nesting Plus under its parent frames it as an upgrade, and five situations built on real intended use cases cut the work of choosing.

Test Name: ID1008 | EU | BYOB | BYOB 2.0: goal-based sticky footer
Experiment description:
Remove the four-node discount ladder from the top of Build Your Own Bundle and move progress into the sticky footer as a single next-goal message, with the max saving carried by a new hero sub-headline. 
List rows unchanged. 

Do-no-harm: primary KPI is CvR staying flat on BYOB-entered sessions, with bundle size and AOV as a signal.

Changes
- Hero - new background image and gains sub-headline "Save up to 20%" — carries the ceiling the ladder used to communicate
- Four-node stepper removed, along with the sticky top band and the redundant 'Buld your Bundle' copy; product list now starts directly under the hero
    - Sticky footer rebuilt, showing one goal state at a time as a pill with sparkle icon: "Add 2 items to start saving" (when user has 0–1 items)
    - "10% off unlocked · Spend £X more for 15%"
    - "15% off unlocked · Spend £X more for 20%"
    - "20% off unlocked!"
- Footer adds a "You'll save £X" line in red above the subtotal
- Subtotal gains a superscript item count
- Expand chevron retained on the bundle summary, but 'Expand' copy removed
- Row UI, swatches, Add pill and See details all unchanged from control

Supporting evidence
- Goal-gradient effect (Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng, 2006) — the core mechanism. Effort accelerates as a goal nears; a single reachable target should raise the rate at which shoppers cross the next threshold.
- Anchoring (BOOM day 5) — the ladder puts €99 in view immediately. For someone holding one €54.95 item that reads as far off, and risks reframing the exercise as expensive rather than rewarding.
- Loss framing — "You'll save £5.99" makes the discount a concrete quantity in hand rather than a percentage in the abstract; "10% unlocked" creates something to protect.
- Proximity / co-location — decision-relevant information beside the decision. The control's progress cue sits at the top of a long scroll, far from the point of commitment.
- Cognitive load — four simultaneous thresholds, two mechanisms and a price ladder is a lot to parse above the fold on mobile.
- Above-fold recovery — removing the sticky top surfaces roughly one extra product on first view, which supports the range exposure that drives bundle size.

Risk - we no logner communicate free shipping
Hypothesis:
IF we replace the four-node ladder with a single next-goal message placed in the sticky footer, 

THEN conversion rate will remain flat while bundle size, threshold-crossing rate and AOV hold or improve,

BECAUSE showing all four thresholds at once anchors on the largest unreached target and makes saving feel distant to a shopper holding one item; a single proximate goal exploits the goal-gradient effect, where effort rises as perceived distance to reward shrinks. Moving the message into the footer also co-locates it with the subtotal and the CTA, so the "is one more item worth it" calculation happens where the shopper is already looking rather than requiring a scroll back to the top.
