Test Name: ID1038 | EU | Cart | Flagship - Full cart - Bundle
Experiment description:
The first full cart re-design: validated elements from the small cart tests combined into one cohesive layout, plus one new lever — a light bundle-up cross-sell offer.

Control — current live cart: free-shipping message, full-price cross-sell carousel, subtotal, single checkout CTA.

V1
- Free-shipping progress bar — new copy, layout and design; visual fill showing remaining spend, flips to an "unlocked" state, persists on scroll
- USP reassurance row below cart items (100-day trial, 2-year warranty)
- Bundle Cross-sell — carousel replaced by a single focused product module with in-module colour selection; item chosen by Visually's "most often paired with" logic
    - Sequential second offer once the first is accepted - no thrid offer
    - Copy: Bundle it and save XX%
    - Bundle discount — accepting applies the discount retroactively across eligible cart items, with reference prices ("Usually €44.95") and a "You save €X" line above subtotal
- Express checkout (Apple Pay etc.) alongside the standard CTA — v2 from ID957; footer non-sticky, sitting at the end of cart content

Offer and discount rules
Eligibility
- Offered item is never a collaboration or limited edition
- Collabs and LE already in the cart don't suppress the module — they count toward the threshold but are charged at full price, labelled Limited edition — full price on the line item
- Discounted module shows one offer, then if taken, a second, and no more
Rate
- ≥€49 → 10%; ≥€69 → 15%. No 20% tier — that stays exclusive to BYOB, and cart copy doesn't mention it
- Eclipse in cart or offer → 10%, hard cap
- Thresholds calculated on the full cart; discount applies to eligible items only (not colabs/LTD editions)
- Recomputes on every cart change, never locks at acceptance

Risk: exclusion-rule behaviour is untested.
Lots of collab and LE stock is live, so many V1 sessions will land on a mixed cart and see a saving smaller than the headline rate.
Mitigation: we never offer a collab or LE item, but a collab or LE already in the cart doesn't block the offer — it counts toward the threshold and stays at full price, labelled Limited edition — always full price. The module never disappears mid-session.
Unknown: whether a partial saving converts as well as a clean one.

---

Already validated in isolation: cross-sell block design (large product image), USP reassurance line, express payments with non-sticky footer.

What this isolates: whether the combined design plus a discounted offer holds or lifts CR and gross profit.

Success: flat or better on CR and gross profit per user is enough to ship the flagship design.
- Follow-up (Big cart 2): identical design, social-proof framing instead of discount — "87% of Dream fans usually add these too", full price throughout, no savings line.
Hypothesis: If we build on two validated cart wins (cross-sell, USP reassurance) by adding progress toward free shipping, a retroactive bundle discount, and express pay, then purchase conversion and gross profit per user will increase — because the cart's remaining barrier is hesitation, not intent — and a retroactive saving makes the add-on feel like a discount earned rather than extra spend.
Additional metrics: Clicks on regular checkout button compared to xpress checkout (apple pay), item added from upsell block

Test Name: ID1041 | EU | Cart | Full cart 2 - Customers also buy
Experiment description:
The cross-sell block and USP reassurance row have already tested positive and are live. This test builds on that baseline rather than re-testing it; prior uplifts are the new baseline, not additive to the effect expected here.

Control: Current live cart. Static free-shipping message, cross-sell carousel at full price, USP reassurance, subtotal, single checkout CTA.

Shared variant foundation (identical in both big cart tests):
- Free-shipping progress bar — visual fill with remaining amount, flipping to an "unlocked" state, persisting on scroll
- USP reassurance moved to per-line-item badges (100-day trial, 2-year warranty)
- Cross-sell reframed from carousel to a single focused product module with in-module colour selection
- Sequential second offer after the first is accepted
- Apple Pay alongside the standard checkout CTA

Big cart Test 2 — Economic incentive: "Bundle it and save 15%". Accepting applies 15% retroactively across the whole cart, with reference prices ("Usually £44.95") and a "You'll save £X" line above subtotal.

Big cart Test 1 — Social proof: "87% of Dream fans usually add these too". Full price throughout, no discount, no savings line. The offer is justified by what similar customers do rather than by price.

What this isolates: whether cart attach is driven by transaction utility (the deal itself as a source of value) or by a descriptive social norm (reduced decision risk through others' behaviour). A wins on volume, B wins on margin per attach — the question is which nets out higher.

This is Test 1
Hypothesis: If we justify the cart cross-sell with a descriptive norm ("87% of Dream fans usually add these too") instead of a price incentive, then attach rate and gross profit per user will increase, because the barrier to a second product isn't price — it's uncertainty about whether it's relevant to someone like them, and evidence of what similar buyers do resolves that at zero margin cost.

Test Name: ID1044 | EU | Homepage | Hero stacked follow-up
Experiment description:
Previous test: ID955 — Homepage Hero Format: Carousel vs Stacked vs Hybrid, mobile, run in EU, USA and AUS [add EU/AUS IDs]. Neither variant was good enough to roll out, least of all in EU, our largest market: stacked came in at −5.9% purchase CR there and hybrid at −3.1%. Pooled across all three markets stacked was −3.8% (~93% likely worse) and hybrid −1.1% (flat). So we iterate rather than roll out.

What we learned
Slide CTR moved a lot and revenue did not. Making slides more visible lifted CTR 2–8x with 100% certainty on nearly every slide, while purchase rate stayed flat or fell. PDP entrance rate did not move either (pooled −0.7%, inconclusive). PLP entrance looked like it rose, but that is the Archive Sale page sitting on a PLP URL path — the extra clicks on the Archive slide alone account for the entire gain, so no real change there.
The read: attention inside the hero is easy to move, and it does not by itself become a product visit or a purchase. The next step has to be about converting hero attention into product entries, not about generating more hero clicks.

Two variations
Both are auto-timed with the pause control available, and both move the evergreen slide from position 5 to position 3 — in the previous test it out-clicked the campaign slide at position 3 in all three markets from a worse position, so its demand is suppressed by placement.
- V1 (design) — visual cleanup, stronger focus on the imagery. Hero height unchanged.
- V2 — same as V1, plus shorter cards so the bestseller product entrance sits higher in the page, and a clear product-linked CTA on each card. Built as a fork of V1, so V1 → V2 isolates card height + CTA.

What we'll learn
- Whether promoting the evergreen slide finally turns its demand into product visits (Control → V1), and on top of that whether a shorter hero with product-linked CTAs converts hero attention into PDP entrances and purchases (V1 → V2). If slide CTR rises again without purchase CR following, that settles it: hero layout is not a revenue lever and we take it off the roadmap.
Hypothesis: If we make the hero visually cleaner and more focused (V1), and shorten the cards while giving each one a clear product-linked CTA (V2), we expect purchase conversion rate (H1) and slider CTR (H2) to increase, because ID955 showed that hero clicks rose sharply while purchase rate, PDP and PLP entrance all stayed flat — the hero produced attention but not qualified product traffic, and it pushed the bestseller product entrance too far down the page.
Dev briefing:
'- Only change the hero format (so no usecase entrys etc, just the top part)
- Same CTR measurement of all slides like in previous test
